items.summary: Turn one client conversation into the priced proposal you send today: their problem in their words, a scoped deliverable list with the exclusions written in, a rate you can defend, and the follow-up and objection replies for everything that happens after you hit send.

inputs.label: What the client needs, in their words
inputs.help: Paste their inquiry, your call notes, the Slack message: whatever they actually wrote or said. Do not tidy it up. The opening of every proposal that wins restates the client's problem in the client's own language, and this box is the only place that language exists.

inputs.label: What you are selling
inputs.help: Sets the market-rate band we price against and the deliverable conventions we write to. Pick "other" and we price from your own stated rate instead of a band, and say so in the document rather than inventing a benchmark.

inputs.label: Project or monthly retainer
inputs.help: "Project" writes a scoped one-off with a deposit structure. "Retainer" scores the relationship first, then writes a monthly offer with a minimum term and a cancellation clause. Leave it blank and we read it off your brief: a defined endpoint reads as project, a recurring need reads as retainer.

inputs.label: Your rate, or what you want to charge
inputs.help: A number, a range, or what you charged them last time. Leave it blank and we price from the market band for your service and show you the arithmetic: we would rather show the maths than quote a figure you cannot defend on a call.

inputs.label: Your history with this client
inputs.help: How long, how many projects, what they paid, whether they pay on time, how their briefs and feedback run, and anything they have said about future work. This is the whole input to the retainer candidate score: eight signals for, five against, and it is what decides whether we tell you to pitch monthly or stay on projects.

inputs.label: What you would actually produce
inputs.help: Counts, formats, turnaround, revision rounds. Exact numbers, not ranges: "10-15 posts" is the single most common way a freelance scope gets eaten. Leave it blank and we propose a scope from the service conventions and mark it for you to check.

inputs.label: Timeline and any deadline driving it
inputs.help: A launch, a season, an event, or just when they want to start. A three-line timeline in a proposal removes more hesitation than another paragraph of approach.

inputs.label: Your relevant experience and results
inputs.help: Client types, platforms, years, and any result you can point at with a real number. This box is the ONLY source for the credibility section: we will not invent a past client or a growth figure, and if you leave it blank we write the short honest version instead.

inputs.label: What the client's business does
inputs.help: Their product, audience, and what they are trying to grow. This is what turns a list of services into an offer aimed at their actual goal.

inputs.label: Who decides, and what you know about budget
inputs.help: Who signs off, whether they are comparing quotes, anything said about money. It changes the close and it decides which objection scripts we write for you.

inputs.label: What they have already pushed back on
inputs.help: "Higher than expected", "can you do less", "we are talking to a few people", "we do not have consistent work". Paste it and we write the reply to the objection you actually got instead of the generic five.

inputs.label: How you want to send it
inputs.help: A full document for a scoped engagement, a short email for a small job, or a packaged rate card when they have asked "what do you charge?". Leave it blank and we pick from the size of the engagement.

inputs.label: Give them tiered options
inputs.help: Builds Starter / Core / Premium with a comparison card, Core marked as recommended. Use it when they have pushed back on price or scope, for a first pitch, one clear option closes faster than three.

inputs.label: Contract terms you already work under
inputs.help: Dispute resolution, IP and usage ownership, confidentiality, late-payment interest, priority access: whatever your contract or your last engagement already says, one per line. Anything you name here is written into the terms list as your term. Anything you leave out is listed as a decision for you to make, because a clause we invented is one a client could hold you to.

items.name: Community Comment Reply Engine
items.summary: Clear a full comment section in the time it used to take to answer five: every reply written in your voice, sorted so the questions get answered first, and the bad-faith ones left alone on purpose.

inputs.label: Paste the comments
inputs.help: One per line, or straight out of YouTube Studio with the usernames attached: either works. Include the spam and the nasty ones; sorting those out and leaving them alone is part of the job, and hiding them from us just means they come back unlabelled. Up to forty at a time.

inputs.label: What the video was about
inputs.help: Title and two or three sentences on what you actually said or showed. This is what turns "great question" into an answer: a reply that references the thing they watched reads as though you watched it too, because you did.

inputs.label: Answers to the questions you get asked constantly
inputs.help: Your gear, your software, your settings, your prices, where you got the thing: one per line as "question: answer". This is the ONLY source we will answer a factual question from. Leave it out and "what mic is that?" gets a warm acknowledgement and a flag for you, rather than a confident guess at a microphone you do not own.

inputs.label: A few replies you have written yourself
inputs.help: Three to five, pasted exactly as you sent them: typos, lowercase, emoji and all. This is worth more than any description of your tone, because how you reply to a comment is not how you write a script. We read the register off these and reuse it.

inputs.label: How you come across in replies
inputs.help: Only used when you have not pasted samples above. Casual is the default because that is what a comment section is; a reply in full sentences with proper capitalisation reads as a brand account, not a person.

inputs.label: Emoji
inputs.help: Sparing is the default: roughly one where it genuinely lands. Getting this wrong is one of the two things that makes a batch of replies read as written by somebody else, the other being length.

inputs.label: How long your replies usually run
inputs.help: match_the_comment is the default and is the source's own rule: a three-word compliment gets a short reply, a four-paragraph story gets a real one. A long reply under a short comment reads as strange, not as generous.

inputs.label: What you want left alone
inputs.help: The default skips both spam and bad-faith comments and tells you why each one was skipped. draft_everything_and_mark_it still refuses to draft an argument: it gives you a single de-escalating line and the note that not replying is usually the better move.

inputs.label: Anything you will not discuss in comments
inputs.help: Politics, a competitor, an ongoing dispute, your income, a family matter. One per line. Comments touching these go to the skip list with the reason, whatever else they say.

inputs.label: One thing you would like people to do
inputs.help: A poll running on your Community tab, a video you would like more eyes on, a question you want answers to. It gets woven into a couple of replies where it genuinely fits and nowhere else: a call to action under every reply is an advert, not a conversation.

items.summary: Find out why your patrons are actually leaving and fix the structure that is losing them: a diagnostic on your real numbers, a rebuilt set of tiers with the arithmetic shown, the delivery rhythm that makes people stay, and the relaunch that changes it all without a walkout.

inputs.label: Your tiers as they stand
inputs.help: One per line: name, price, and exactly what a member at that level gets. Copy it off your own page rather than summarising it; the value-overlap check reads the benefit lists word for word, and "behind-the-scenes photos" appearing in two tiers is the kind of thing a summary smooths over and a diagnostic needs to see.

inputs.label: How many members are in each tier, and what that earns
inputs.help: "$3 tier: 45 people, $135/mo" per line, or just the counts if you would rather we do the multiplication. Every figure in the audit comes from this and nowhere else: we will not estimate a patron count, because the projection is computed from it and a made-up starting number makes every number after it wrong.

inputs.label: Where the membership runs
inputs.help: Patreon is the default. This is a real constraint, not a label: YouTube caps you at five tiers and rewards members-only videos, Substack's paid tier needs a different format rather than more posts, Ko-fi audiences expect something simpler. We will not recommend a structure your platform cannot run.

inputs.label: What you know about people leaving
inputs.help: How many leave a month, which tiers they leave from, anything they told you on the way out, and whether it spiked after something. Rough is fine. Leave it blank and the audit reasons from your tier distribution instead and says which parts of the diagnosis are inference rather than data, which is the honest version, not a worse one.

inputs.label: Which way the numbers have moved
inputs.help: Over the last six months or so. Flat and slowly_declining need different fixes: flat is usually a conversion or a top-tier problem, declining is usually a delivery problem: so this changes the diagnosis more than it looks like it should.

inputs.label: How big your audience is outside the membership
inputs.help: Subscribers, downloads a month, list size, followers. Used for the conversion-rate check against the 1-5% band that most creators land in. Being under it is a marketing problem and being over it is a pricing one, and they have opposite fixes: so without this the audit cannot tell you which one you have.

inputs.label: What members actually get, and how often
inputs.help: Be honest about the frequency, including the months you missed. The most common cause of steady drip churn is not the tiers at all. It is that nobody can see what they are paying for, and an audit built on your intended schedule instead of your real one diagnoses the wrong thing.

inputs.label: Hours a week you can give member-only work
inputs.help: Hard cap on what the new top tier is allowed to promise. Every benefit in the restructure gets a time cost attached and the total has to fit inside this: a premium tier you cannot deliver churns worse than the one you have.

inputs.label: What you actually want to change
inputs.help: These pull in different directions: a lower entry price wins members and lowers your average, a stronger top tier does the reverse. Picking one gets you a sharper restructure; all_three gets you a sequenced plan that says which to fix first and why.

inputs.label: Whether you offer annual
inputs.help: Worth asking because the source's strongest single retention lever is here: annual members churn far less, and because recommending it on a platform that does not offer it wastes the recommendation.

inputs.label: Anything you are not willing to change
inputs.help: A price you promised would never rise, a benefit people joined for, a tier named after an in-joke. One per line. The restructure works around these rather than quietly dropping them, and where one is genuinely the problem we say so and leave the decision with you.

inputs.label: When you would announce the change
inputs.help: A date or a rough window. Used for the grandfathering period and the "new pricing goes live on" line. Leave it blank and the plan runs in relative weeks: we will not put a deadline in your announcement that you did not set.

inputs.label: Your show and who listens

inputs.label: Format
inputs.help: Defaults to interview. Solo and co-host skip the guest questions and get an opening line written as a direct address instead; roundtable gets a moderator framework with rotation and tension prompts.

inputs.label: Target length
inputs.help: Defaults to forty-five minutes. This sets the segment count directly: twenty gets three segments, forty-five gets five: because a 45-minute episode split three ways is a fifteen-minute segment nobody can hold.

inputs.label: Guest name and role
inputs.help: Leave it blank for a solo episode and you still get a full run: the guest step builds the scoring rubric for who you should be targeting, and the outreach kit writes the pitch you send the next one.

inputs.label: What you know about the guest
inputs.help: Their bio, recent work, a talk or article, past podcast appearances, anything they have said that you want to press on. Paste it rather than summarising it. This is the only source we will quote them from: we do not look anything up, and we will never invent a book, a job or an appearance to make a pitch land. Leave it blank and you get a short list of exactly what to go and find, with the pitch written around a marked gap.

inputs.label: What a listener can do after this episode
inputs.help: One thing, stated as an action. Every segment gets checked against it, and the segments that do not move a listener toward it get cut or flagged.

inputs.label: What makes this different from the other fifty episodes on this topic
inputs.help: A disagreement, a specific case, a number you have that nobody else does. Leave it blank and we propose the angle and show our reasoning so you can overrule it.

inputs.label: Segments or subtopics you already have
inputs.help: One per line. If you give us more than the length allows we say so and recommend what to cut or combine rather than cramming them all in.

inputs.label: What the last episode covered
inputs.help: Used to open with a short callback and close with a forward tease, which is the cheapest retention move on a series and the one most often skipped.

inputs.label: What you want listeners to do at the end
inputs.help: Exactly one gets written out verbatim. A list of options at the end of an episode converts on none of them.

inputs.label: Where you are with this guest
inputs.help: Not contacted gets the cold pitch and the three follow-ups. Confirmed gets the booking confirmation and the pre-recording briefing email instead. No guest gets the templates for the next one.

inputs.label: How much of a public figure they are
inputs.help: Sets the formality and length of the follow-ups. A major public figure's inbox is managed by someone else, so every touch gets shorter and the ask gets easier to say yes to.

inputs.label: Numbers or names you can honestly cite
inputs.help: Downloads an episode, subscriber count, a guest people would recognise, a milestone. These are the only figures that can appear in a pitch: we will not round them up or invent one. A small show described honestly outperforms an inflated number that a guest can check.

inputs.label: Anything off limits
inputs.help: Controversies, work they have moved on from, subjects they have asked not to cover. These get a handle-with-care note with a redirect line, rather than being silently omitted where you might wander into them live.

inputs.label: How you sound on air
inputs.help: Defaults to conversational. This governs the opening line and the intro script most of all, since those are the two you read word for word.

inputs.label: Your show, in a couple of sentences

"A weekly solo-and-occasional-interview show about freelance consulting, for people two to five years in" beats "a business podcast": every episode on the map has to earn its place with that listener.

inputs.label: Why a season, and why this one
inputs.help: The topic, question, or shift in your own thinking that made you want to plan a season instead of picking a topic each week. This becomes the throughline every episode has to serve. Half-formed is fine: "something about what breaks when you try to hire" is enough to work from.

inputs.label: Which season this is
inputs.help: "Season 4", "the first real season", or leave it blank. Only used for naming and for the callback beats in the promo plan.

inputs.label: How many episodes
inputs.help: Ten is the default and the shape most solo shows finish. Eight is the honest answer if you have never completed a season. Twelve needs either a co-host or batch recording.

inputs.label: Formats you can actually produce
inputs.help: Solo, interview, co-host, listener Q&A, panel, narrative, live. One per line. We never put a format on the map you did not name: twelve interview slots on a show that cannot book guests is the failure this question exists to prevent.

inputs.label: Guests you can realistically book this season
inputs.help: Be honest rather than optimistic. This number caps how many guest-dependent episodes go on the map, and guest-dependent episodes are the ones that get flagged as at-risk.

inputs.label: Topics or guests you already know you want in
inputs.help: One per line. These get placed where they serve the arc rather than where they land alphabetically, and anything that fights the throughline gets flagged rather than quietly dropped.

inputs.label: What earlier seasons or episodes already covered
inputs.help: Titles, themes, or a rough list. Used to keep the new season off ground you have already worked, and to write the "what this season is NOT about" line that stops episodes drifting later.

inputs.label: How often you publish
inputs.help: Weekly is the default. Biweekly is what most solo hosts can actually hold for ten straight episodes, and a calendar you keep beats a cadence you announce.

inputs.label: How long one episode really takes you, start to finish
inputs.help: Recording time, editing time, and how long guests take to get on your calendar: your real numbers, not the good week. "Record 90 min, edit 4 hours over 3 days, guests take 3 weeks to schedule" is exactly right. Leave it blank and we state the model we assumed at the top of the calendar so you can correct it in one line.

inputs.label: When the season starts (or has to finish)
inputs.help: A start date, or a finale date if you are working backward from something fixed. Blank means we build the calendar in relative weeks from your first recording block.

inputs.label: Weeks you already know you lose
inputs.help: Travel, holidays, a launch, anything that will eat a production week. These are where seasons slip, so the calendar routes around them instead of pretending they are not coming.

inputs.label: Who does the work
inputs.help: Solo means the lead times stay long and the calendar recommends batch recording. An editor changes the edit-complete column and nothing else.

inputs.label: Where the show is
inputs.help: A new show gets the launch checklist: trailer, directory submissions, the first-three-episodes plan. An ongoing show gets a promo arc that assumes an audience already exists, which is a different plan, not a shorter one.

inputs.label: Where you actually post
inputs.help: Instagram, X, TikTok, YouTube Shorts, LinkedIn, a newsletter: only the ones you genuinely use. We would rather write four good beats for two platforms than a plan across five you will abandon in week two.

inputs.label: Promo posts a week you can sustain
inputs.help: Through the whole season, not launch week. The plan is sized to this number and includes a repeatable weekly template so the middle stretch takes under ten minutes.

inputs.label: Where your numbers are now
inputs.help: Roughly what an episode does and how big your following is per platform. Starting small is completely fine and changes how aggressive the launch push is. These are the only audience figures that can appear anywhere in the output: we never invent one.

inputs.label: How the show sounds
inputs.help: Mostly matters for the trailer script, which is the one artifact here you read aloud. Pick match_my_show if you described the show's voice above.

inputs.label: Your show and its niche

inputs.label: What an episode actually does
inputs.help: Downloads per episode in the first thirty days, and whether that number is growing, flat, or falling. Round numbers are fine, guesses are not: every rate on your card is computed from this and it is the first thing a buyer asks for. Trend matters as much as size; a growing show prices better than a plateaued one twice its size.

inputs.label: How often you publish
inputs.help: Sets episodes per month, which is the multiplier on every package price. Weekly by default.

inputs.label: Newsletter list, if you have one
inputs.help: A list is a separate line item priced at its own CPM and it is the cheapest thing to add to a package. Leave it blank if you do not have one.

inputs.label: Anything that shows people actually listen
inputs.help: Reviews, average completion, a community, social following, replies. Buyers weigh this third after alignment and volume, and it is how a small show outbids a bigger one. Only what you can point at: we never estimate an engagement number.

inputs.label: Sponsorships you have already done
inputs.help: Brand, what they paid, what they got, whether they renewed. Renewals are the single strongest thing in a pitch, and past rates stop the new card contradicting a number a buyer has already seen.

inputs.label: What you want this to earn
inputs.help: Changes which streams get recommended and in what order, not what your show is worth. The rate card is the same either way.

inputs.label: Products you genuinely use and would recommend
inputs.help: One per line. These are the affiliate and sponsor candidates worth chasing, and if you have no sponsor yet they are what the ad scripts are written for, so you have a house read ready.

inputs.label: The sponsor, if you already have one
inputs.help: Brand name and what they do, in plain terms. Leave it blank and the ad scripts are written for your own offer or an affiliate instead: we do not invent a sponsor to have something to write.

inputs.label: What the sponsor requires you to say
inputs.help: Paste their brief exactly: mandatory claims, the offer, the promo code, the URL, and any legal or disclosure language. Every one of these survives the rewrite word for word, and anything that clashes with how you talk gets flagged back to you rather than quietly dropped.

inputs.label: Your own experience with the product
inputs.help: What you actually use it for, what it replaced, what it fixed, how long you have had it. This is the line that converts, and it is the one line we will not write for you: leave it blank and the script marks the spot and tells you exactly what to say from your own use. We will never put an experience you did not report into your mouth.

inputs.label: Which placements you sell
inputs.help: All by default. Each placement gets its own opening and closing move rather than one script trimmed three ways, because a pre-roll and a post-roll are talking to listeners in completely different states.

inputs.label: How ads go into your episodes
inputs.help: Baked-in ads stay in the file forever and carry a premium over dynamic ones for exactly that reason. Not sure is a fine answer and the card prices both.

inputs.label: How you actually talk
inputs.help: Two or three sentences in your normal register, straight off a transcript if you have one. This beats any tone preset for the ad scripts, which are the artifacts where sounding like a voiceover artist is the whole failure.

inputs.label: Anything you will not say on air
inputs.help: Overclaims, competitor comparisons, categories you will not take money from, a register that does not fit the show. These are honoured absolutely, and where one clashes with something the sponsor requires we say so rather than choosing for you.

inputs.label: What you promised against what you shipped

inputs.label: Where and how it ran
inputs.help: Sets which reach metrics are meaningful and which benchmarks apply. A story frame and a dedicated video are not compared to the same numbers.

inputs.label: What people actually said
inputs.help: Three to five real comments, pasted exactly, including any criticism worth addressing. This is the section brands forward internally: "I already ordered this, saw it on your channel" is worth more than any metric. Quotes are used verbatim or trimmed with an ellipsis, never rewritten, because the brand can open the post and read them.

inputs.label: What this format normally does for you

inputs.label: Anything you projected when you sold the deal
inputs.help: Numbers from the media kit or the pitch that the brand is holding you to. The report compares against them explicitly, including where the result came in under: the brand has this document open next to yours.

inputs.label: What the campaign was worth
inputs.help: Used only to compute the brand's cost per redemption, which is the number that justifies rebooking you. It never appears in the report itself: the source rule is absolute, a recap that quotes a price stops being a recap and becomes an invoice.

inputs.label: How this brand talks to you
inputs.help: An enterprise software company on a first campaign and a DTC startup you text with expect completely different documents. This changes the register of the whole report, not just the greeting.

inputs.label: Who this is going to
inputs.help: The person at the brand who will open it. Leave it blank and the greeting is written without a name rather than with a bracketed placeholder.

inputs.label: Anything coming up worth pointing at
inputs.help: A product launch, a seasonal push, their Q4 planning window, a use case this campaign surfaced. The closing proposal ties to something real or it stays general: we do not invent a launch to have something to suggest.

inputs.label: Is this early data?
inputs.help: On if you are sending at seven or fourteen days rather than waiting for final numbers. Sending early is the right call and this makes it honest: the summary states the age of the data and commits to a follow-up with updated figures.

inputs.help: Paste their brief, email or DM exactly as it arrived, however vague. inputs.label: The fee already agreed, if there is one

inputs.help: Usage period, which channels, whether they want whitelisting or spark ads, whether they want you off competitors. inputs.label: What you are selling, and to whom

inputs.help: The number and any payment plan. Decides how much objection handling the offer segment needs: a $97 product and a $3,000 cohort do not get the same close. Leave it blank and we mark every price slot so you can fill them in one pass.

inputs.label: Where you are running it
inputs.help: Changes the tech checklist and which engagement markers are even possible: a platform without native polls gets chat prompts instead of [POLL] cues rather than cues you cannot run.

inputs.label: Who is registering
inputs.help: What they already know, what they have already tried, and what they are afraid of. This is where the objection bank gets its specificity: generic objections get generic answers, and generic answers do not close anyone.

inputs.label: Have you taught this before

inputs.label: Results, case studies and stories you can actually cite
